    Beta Diversity Partitioning (Baselga Framework)

    BetaPart.Rd

    Calculates multiple-site beta diversity partitioning into turnover and nestedness (or balanced variation and gradient) components using the framework of Baselga (2010, 2012, 2013). Returns a summary table with overall partitioning values across all sites.

    BetaPart(DF, index = "sorensen", shape = "w")

    Arguments

    DF

    A data.frame containing species data. The first column should contain station names (if shape = "w") or species names (if shape = "l").

    index

    Type of beta diversity index to use:

    • "sorensen" - Sorensen dissimilarity (presence-absence, default)

    • "jaccard" - Jaccard dissimilarity (presence-absence)

    • "bray" - Bray-Curtis dissimilarity (abundance-based)

    • "ruzicka" - Ruzicka dissimilarity (abundance-based)

    shape

    Data format specification (default = "w"):

    • "w" - Wide format: stations in rows, species in columns (first column = station names) (default)

    • "l" - Long format: species in rows, stations in columns (first column = species names)

    Value

    A data.frame with three rows and three columns:

    • Component - Name of the beta diversity component

    • Beta - Numeric value of the component (0 to 1)

    • Interpretation - Brief explanation of what the component measures

    The three components depend on the index used:

    For Sorensen: Total (betaSOR), Turnover (betaSIM), Nestedness (betaSNE)

    For Jaccard: Total (betaJAC), Turnover (betaJTU), Nestedness (betaJNE)

    For Bray-Curtis: Total (betaBRA), Balanced (betaBAL), Gradient (betaGRA)

    For Ruzicka: Total (betaRUZ), Balanced (betaBAL), Gradient (betaGRA)

    Details

    This function calculates multiple-site beta diversity partitioning following the additive framework of Baselga (2010, 2012, 2013). It returns a single set of values representing the overall partitioning across all sites in the dataset.

    For presence-absence data (Sorensen/Jaccard):

    Total beta diversity is additively partitioned as: $$\beta_{total} = \beta_{turnover} + \beta_{nestedness}$$

    • Total (betaSOR/betaJAC) - Overall compositional dissimilarity among all sites. Values close to 1 indicate high differentiation; close to 0 indicate similar communities.

    • Turnover (betaSIM/betaJTU) - Measures species replacement between sites. High values indicate communities differ primarily due to species substitution. Reflects deterministic processes like environmental filtering, dispersal limitation, or competitive exclusion.

    • Nestedness (betaSNE/betaJNE) - Measures species loss/gain without replacement. High values indicate some sites contain subsets of species from other sites. Reflects stochastic processes like colonization-extinction dynamics, habitat loss, or ordered extinctions along environmental gradients.

    For abundance data (Bray-Curtis/Ruzicka):

    Total beta diversity is additively partitioned as: $$\beta_{total} = \beta_{balanced} + \beta_{gradient}$$

    • Total (betaBRA/betaRUZ) - Overall abundance-based dissimilarity among all sites.

    • Balanced variation (betaBAL) - Abundance changes balanced across species. Analogous to turnover in presence-absence framework. Reflects reciprocal abundance changes among species (some increase while others decrease).

    • Abundance gradient (betaGRA) - Unidirectional abundance changes. Analogous to nestedness in presence-absence framework. Reflects consistent abundance gradients across sites (e.g., productivity or disturbance gradients).

    Interpretation guidelines:

    • All values range from 0 to 1

    • betatotal = betaturnover + betanestedness (additive partitioning)

    • If Turnover/Balanced >> Nestedness/Gradient: Replacement processes dominate

    • If Nestedness/Gradient >> Turnover/Balanced: Nested patterns or gradients dominate

    • Balanced partitioning suggests both processes contribute equally

    Choosing an index:

    • Use Sorensen for presence-absence data (most common, insensitive to richness differences)

    • Use Jaccard for presence-absence when richness differences matter

    • Use Bray-Curtis for abundance data (most common in ecology)

    • Use Ruzicka for abundance data (quantitative form of Jaccard)

    Understanding the partitioning helps identify ecological processes structuring benthic communities and guides interpretation of diversity patterns.

    References

    Baselga, A. (2010). Partitioning the turnover and nestedness components of beta diversity. Global Ecology and Biogeography, 19(1), 134-143. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1466-8238.2009.00490.x

    Baselga, A. (2012). The relationship between species replacement, dissimilarity derived from nestedness, and nestedness. Global Ecology and Biogeography, 21(12), 1223-1232. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1466-8238.2011.00756.x

    Baselga, A. (2013). Separating the two components of abundance-based dissimilarity: balanced changes in abundance vs. abundance gradients. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 4(6), 552-557. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12029

    Baselga, A. & Orme, C.D.L. (2012). betapart: an R package for the study of beta diversity. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 3(5), 808-812. https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.12110

    See also

    BetaDiv for LCBD/SCBD analysis using adespatial, beta.multi for presence-absence partitioning, beta.multi.abund for abundance-based partitioning

    Examples

    # Example 1: Presence-absence with Sorensen (default)
data_wide <- data.frame(
  Station = c("St1", "St2", "St3", "St4"),
  Capitella = c(1, 1, 0, 0),
  Owenia = c(1, 0, 1, 0),
  Nephtys = c(0, 0, 1, 1),
  Lumbrineris = c(0, 1, 1, 0)
)
BetaPart(data_wide, index = "sorensen", shape = "w")
#>              Component      Beta                           Interpretation
#> 1      Total (BetaSOR) 0.6666667      Overall dissimilarity between sites
#> 2   Turnover (BetaSIM) 0.5555556 Dissimilarity due to species replacement
#> 3 Nestedness (BetaSNE) 0.1111111   Dissimilarity due to species loss/gain

# Example 2: Presence-absence with Jaccard
result_jac <- BetaPart(data_wide, index = "jaccard", shape = "w")
print(result_jac)
#>              Component       Beta                           Interpretation
#> 1      Total (BetaJAC) 0.80000000      Overall dissimilarity between sites
#> 2   Turnover (BetaJTU) 0.71428571 Dissimilarity due to species replacement
#> 3 Nestedness (BetaJNE) 0.08571429   Dissimilarity due to species loss/gain

# Example 3: Abundance-based with Bray-Curtis
data_wide <- data.frame(
  Station = c("St1", "St2", "St3", "St4"),
  Capitella = c(45, 12, 0, 0),
  Owenia = c(23, 18, 45, 50),
  Nephtys = c(12, 0, 23, 10),
  Lumbrineris = c(0, 15, 12, 5)
)
result_bray <- BetaPart(data_wide, index = "bray", shape = "w")
print(result_bray)
#>            Component       Beta
#> 1    Total (BetaBRA) 0.58610272
#> 2 Balanced (BetaBAL) 0.49446494
#> 3 Gradient (BetaGRA) 0.09163777
#>                                     Interpretation
#> 1              Overall dissimilarity between sites
#> 2 Dissimilarity due to balanced abundance turnover
#> 3         Dissimilarity due to abundance gradients

# Example 4: Abundance-based with Ruzicka
BetaPart(data_wide, index = "ruzicka", shape = "w")
#>            Component       Beta
#> 1    Total (BetaRUZ) 0.73904762
#> 2 Balanced (BetaBAL) 0.66172840
#> 3 Gradient (BetaGRA) 0.07731922
#>                                     Interpretation
#> 1              Overall dissimilarity between sites
#> 2 Dissimilarity due to balanced abundance turnover
#> 3         Dissimilarity due to abundance gradients

# Example 5: Long format data
data_long <- data.frame(
  Species = c("Capitella", "Owenia", "Nephtys"),
  St1 = c(1, 0, 1),
  St2 = c(1, 1, 0),
  St3 = c(0, 0, 1)
)
BetaPart(data_long, index = "sorensen", shape = "l")
#>              Component Beta                           Interpretation
#> 1      Total (BetaSOR)  0.6      Overall dissimilarity between sites
#> 2   Turnover (BetaSIM)  0.5 Dissimilarity due to species replacement
#> 3 Nestedness (BetaSNE)  0.1   Dissimilarity due to species loss/gain

# Example 6: Interpreting results
result <- BetaPart(data_wide, index = "bray", shape = "w")
# High Balanced (betaBAL) suggests reciprocal abundance changes
# High Gradient (betaGRA) suggests unidirectional abundance patterns
